_comment: Storyboard for the Grade 4 Science unit lecture film, Lesson 13 The Paper Spinner. Rendered by tools/create-ehel-unit-lecture.js. See lecture-video/BRIEF.md. This lesson is one whole investigation rather than a body of content, so its chapters are the investigation's own steps, in the order LESSON.lecture and the lesson's steps take them: the question and which enquiry answers it, the variables of a fair test, the equipment and its standard units, the three drops of each spinner, the table and the dot plot, and the conclusion. The pictures are the lesson's own: its five enquiry bins, its three variable bins, its kit list, and above all ART.sim('spinner', 'draw', n, y, big, m), the drawing the child drops and times two steps later.
title: The Paper Spinner
subtitle: Grade 4 Science
objectives: Ask scientific questions that can be investigated.
Know that there are five main types of scientific enquiry (research, fair testing, observing over time, identifying and classifying, and pattern seeking).
Make a prediction describing some possible outcomes of an enquiry.
Identify variables that need to be taken into account when doing a fair test.
Choose equipment from a provided selection and use it appropriately.
Describe how repeated measurements and/or observations can give more reliable data.
Take measurements in standard units, describing the advantage of standard units over non-standard units.
Collect and record observations and/or measurements in tables and diagrams.
Identify whether results support, or do not support, a prediction.
Make a conclusion from results and relate it to the scientific question being investigated.
Present and interpret results using tables, bar charts and dot plots.

beats.say: A paper spinner falls, turning as it goes. Does a bigger one fall more slowly?
Today you find out the way a scientist does: one whole investigation.
Every investigation starts with a question you can actually test.
Ours is this: does a spinner with bigger wings fall more slowly?
There are five types of scientific enquiry. The question tells you which.
Research. Fair testing. Observing over time. Classifying. Pattern seeking.
We change one thing and see what happens. So ours is a fair test.
A variable is anything in the test that could change.
You change one variable. Ours is the size of the wings.
You measure one variable. Ours is how long it takes to fall.

at.fall: how long it takes to fall

beats.say: Every other variable stays the same: the height, the paper, the paperclip, the person dropping.
Change two things at once, and you cannot tell which one made the difference.

scenes.heading: The right kit, the right units

beats.say: Choose your equipment before you start. Each job needs the right tool.
To time the fall, take a stopwatch. It reads in seconds.
To set the drop height, take a tape measure. It reads in centimetres.
Seconds and centimetres are standard units: the same for everyone, so anybody can check.
Predict first. Which spinner takes longer to fall, the small one or the big one?
Drop it once and you get one number. Was your thumb slow? Did a draught catch it?
One measurement can be wrong. So drop each spinner three times, from the same height.
The small spinner gave 2.1, then 2.3, then 2.0 seconds.
The spinner with bigger wings gave 2.8, then 3.0, then 2.7 seconds.
Close, but not the same. Small differences are normal. Three close numbers are reliable.

scenes.heading: A table, then a dot plot

beats.say: Write each drop down as it happens, in a table, in seconds.
Drop one took 2.1 seconds, drop two 2.3, and drop three 2.0.
Now a dot plot: one dot for each measurement, above its own time.
The three dots pile up close to 2.1 seconds. An odd one would stand alone.
The small spinner took about 2.1 seconds. The bigger wings took about 2.8.
Two clusters, and the bigger wings took longer on every single drop.
That is the pattern: bigger wings, slower fall. It matches your prediction.
So the conclusion answers the question you asked, and the repeats make it reliable.
A fair test changes one thing and keeps every other thing the same.
Choose the right kit, measure in standard units, and repeat every measurement.
Plot your drops as dots, and let the cluster answer the question you asked.
